_about: The sin hub (second round, 2026-10-25), built the way faith and forgiveness are: the rows are defined by the Hebrew and Greek, a noun row by the words standing in the noun's verse (or by hand where the text sets a group apart), a verb row by hand where the frames are silent, and a verse sits in every row it fits (match: all). Reworked the same day on the owner's word that iniquity, transgression and sin are close to interchangeable: the text sets three Hebrew words for wrongdoing side by side (Exod 34:7), so עָוֺן (iniquity) and פֶּשַׁע / פָּשַׁע (transgression, rebel) are now the hub's own words beside the sin family and their verses fill the rows by the same rules; the page shows them together and never says they are one word. The words are the sin family in both testaments and are not pooled as one: the Hebrew nouns חַטָּאת, חֵטְא, חֲטָאָה, חַטָּאָה and the Aramaic חֲטָא and חַטָּאָה, together with עָוֺן and פֶּשַׁע; the Greek ἁμαρτία and ἁμάρτημα, with παράβασις and παραβάτης (transgression, transgressor); the verbs חָטָא, פָּשַׁע, ἁμαρτάνω and προαμαρτάνω; the adjectives חַטָּא, ἁμαρτωλός and ἀναμάρτητος. A word counts in a verse only where MACULA's English gloss there is a word of wrongdoing (sin, iniquity, guilt, transgression, rebellion, offense, crime; see _sense_why): חָטָא also means 'purify' (Num 8:21; Ps 51:7), 'bear the loss' (Gen 31:39) and 'miss' (Judg 20:16), עָוֺן also 'punishment' (Gen 4:13), פָּשַׁע also a nation's revolt (2 Kgs 3:5); the sense rule drops those. The Hebrew חַטָּאת is also the sin offering; its own row says so. Different words the English also calls sin (ἀνομία, παράπτωμα, ἀγνόημα) are named apart under 'Other words', and the first row sets sin beside them. The rows run from the Law and the Prophets to the Gospels and letters. Three groups of rows are contested between Christian traditions and the page takes no side in any: who bears a person's sin, in the sense readers call original sin and inherited guilt (three rows side by side); how sin holds a person and how the text speaks of resisting it, which readers sometimes call total depravity (three rows side by side); whether a believer sins (three rows side by side) and the sin that leads to death or is not forgiven (one row). titles.noun: What the text says of sin, iniquity and transgression

_words_why: The card lists six words (h2403, h2399, h2401, h2402, g266, and h5512). h5512 סִין is the wilderness of Sin (Exod 16:1), a place name the lexicon glosses 'sin' by sound, and is not a word for wrongdoing; it is left out here (the card lists it, which the card's owner should read). Added in the first round: the verbs חָטָא (219 verses, 156 in this sense) and ἁμαρτάνω (37), προαμαρτάνω 'sinned before' (2 Cor 12:21; 13:2); the adjectives חַטָּא, ἁμαρτωλός and ἀναμάρτητος (John 8:7, 'without sin'); ἁμάρτημα (Mark 3:28-29 and three more); and the Aramaic חֲטָא (Dan 4:27, 'break away from your sins') and חַטָּאָה (Ezra 6:17, a sin offering). Added in the rework of 2026-10-25 (the owner: iniquity, transgression and sin are close to interchangeable; the text itself uses the three as a set, Exod 34:7; Ps 32:1-5; Ps 51:1-3; Lev 16:21): עָוֺן h5771 'iniquity' (231 verses, which the Berean prints 'iniquity', 'guilt' and, in a few, 'sin' or 'punishment'), פֶּשַׁע h6588 'transgression' (the Berean prints 'transgression', 'rebellion', 'offense'), the verb פָּשַׁע h6586 'transgress, rebel', and the Greek παράβασις g3847 'transgression' (Rom 2:23; 4:15; 5:14; Gal 3:19; 1 Tim 2:14; Heb 2:2; 9:15) and παραβάτης g3848 'transgressor' (Rom 2:25, 27; Gal 2:18; Jas 2:9, 11). Kept in 'Other words', not in the rows: ἀνομία g458 'lawlessness' and παράπτωμα g3900 'trespass'. Reason: the rows' labels are the Berean's own words (sin, iniquity, transgression), and ἀνομία and παράπτωμα are words the Berean prints 'lawlessness', 'iniquity' (Heb 1:9), 'trespass', 'transgression' (Rom 5:15-18), so letting their verses fill the rows by rule would put 'trespass' and 'lawlessness' under labels that do not say them; the rows plainly do want them only where they stand beside a sin word, and there the first row carries them by hand and by rule (Eph 2:1 'trespasses and sins'; Rom 4:7 and Heb 8:12; 10:17 'lawless deeds'; 1 John 3:4 'sin is lawlessness'). The negations are not counted, nor are ἁμαρτία's adverbs. παραβαίνω 'to go beyond, transgress' (Matt 15:2-3) is left out: its verses are mostly breaking a tradition or the commandment of God, not named wrongdoing as such, and the hub did not ask for it.
_sense_why: Measured on MACULA's English gloss in each verse (2026-10-25). First round, the sin family: kept gloss 'sin', 'sinned', 'sinning', 'sinful', 'sinner', 'sin offering'; dropped חָטָא as 'purify' or 'cleanse' (63 verses, among them Lev 8:15, 14:49, Num 8:21, 19:12, Ps 51:7), as 'bear the loss' (Gen 31:39, 43:9, 44:32), as 'miss' (Judg 20:16, Prov 8:36, 19:2) and as 'offend' (Gen 40:1, 2 Kgs 18:14); 11 noun verses whose gloss is 'guilt', 'punishment', 'offense', 'failure' or 'purification' (Gen 41:9 'my failures', Lev 19:17 and 22:9 'guilt', Num 8:7 'water of purification', Prov 10:16 and Zech 14:19 'punishment', Eccl 10:4 'great offenses'). Put back by hand (sense_keep) where the Berean itself prints 'sin' although the gloss does not: Deut 15:9, Deut 21:22, Ezek 23:49 and Eccl 5:6. THE REWORK widened the pattern with the English glosses of עָוֺן and פֶּשַׁע: 'iniquity', 'guilt' (the gloss of Ps 32:5 'forgave the guilt of my sin', Jer 3:13, Jer 33:8, Ezek 18:19, Jer 32:18, where the Berean's own word is guilt or iniquity), 'transgression', 'rebellion', 'rebelled', 'offense', 'crime'. Because the pattern is one for every word, three of the first round's drops came back and are dropped again by hand with their reasons (sense_drop): Lev 19:17 and 22:9 (חֵטְא, 'guilt' in the sense of incurring guilt, the Berean 'incur guilt') and Eccl 10:4 ('great offenses'). Left out: עָוֺן as 'punishment' (Gen 4:13 'My punishment is more than I can bear'; Job 19:29 'punishments of the sword') -- the gloss 'punishment' is not in the pattern, so those verses are not counted; this is the owner's brief (keep the sense of wrongdoing; where it is the punishment, say what was done): the verses are neither placed in a row nor shown under a label that says 'sin'. Lam 4:6 ('The punishment of the daughter of my people is greater than that of Sodom') stays in the first row, because its other word, חַטָּאת, passes the sense rule there. Also dropped by hand: פָּשַׁע as a nation's revolt against its overlord (1 Kgs 12:19; 2 Kgs 1:1; 3:5, 7; 8:20, 22; 2 Chr 10:19; 21:8, 10: 'rebelled' of Israel against David's house, Moab against Israel, Edom and Libnah against Judah) and Prov 18:19 (the verb of the brother who was wronged, 'offended').

rows.label: Iniquity, transgression and sin side by side; trespass, lawlessness, wickedness
rows.note: The text sets three Hebrew words for wrongdoing side by side; this page shows them together.עָוֺן is the Berean's “iniquity” (and, in some verses, “guilt”); פֶּשַׁע is “transgression” or “rebellion”; חַטָּאת and its kin are “sin”. Exod 34:7 sets them in one list, “forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin” (עָוֺן, פֶּשַׁע, חַטָּאָה); Ps 32:1-5 and Ps 51:1-3 run through them again, and in Lev 16:21 the high priest confesses “all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins”. Each example is marked with the word it stands on, and a row whose label rests on one of the words says so; the Berean's English does not always follow the Hebrew word (Deut 19:15 has three Hebrew words for wrongdoing in one verse, עָוֺן, חַטָּאת and חֵטְא, and the Berean prints “wrongdoing or sin ... offense”). The page does not say that the three are one word. In Greek the pairing is ἁμαρτία “sin” beside ἀνομία “lawlessness”, παράπτωμα “trespass”, ἀδικία “unrighteousness” and παράβασις “transgression”: in 1 John 3:4 the text itself says “sin is lawlessness”, the one verse that says one word is the other; the other Greek verses set the words beside each other (Eph 2:1; Rom 4:7; Heb 8:12), as the Hebrew verses do (Exod 34:7; Ps 32:5).
rows._why: rework 2026-10-25: the first round made this row a hand list of 73 verses (the rule: a sin word and one of these words in the same verse, and Exod 34:7 added by hand because the rule missed it). Now עָוֺן and פֶּשַׁע are the hub's own words, so the row is a rule: a word of the hub stands within six words of another of these in the same phrase (the text's lists, 'iniquity and transgression and sin'), and the 73 verses stay as 'add' (they are the pairs standing in different phrases of one verse, Ps 32:5), with twelve pairs read in the Berean and added: Num 14:18, Job 7:21, 14:17, 31:33, Ps 65:3, 89:32, 107:17, Isa 50:1, 53:5, Ezek 18:30, Jer 33:8, Mic 7:18. חַטָּאת is left out of the rule's partner list so that 'a sin for a sin offering' (Lev 4) is not taken for a pair. Exod 34:7's sin word is חַטָּאָה (h2402); the data files spell the lemma of עָוֺן two ways, so both spellings are in the rule. 1 John 3:4 is the first example (review 2026-10-25) so that the one verse that says the words are one thing is not lost among those that set them beside each other

rows.label: Confessing sin, iniquity, transgression
rows.note: The verses where sin is confessed, in the Law, the Psalms, Proverbs, the prayers of Nehemiah and Daniel, the baptism of John and the letters. Lev 16:21 is the high priest confessing the Israelites' iniquities, rebellious acts and sins over the live goat; Lev 26:40 is “confess their iniquity and that of their fathers”; Ps 32:5 has all three words (“my sin”, “my iniquity”, “my transgressions”); Prov 28:13 sets the one who “conceals his sins” (פֶּשַׁע, transgressions) beside the one who “confesses and renounces them”; Jer 3:13 asks Israel to “acknowledge your guilt” (the Berean's word for עָוֺן there). Where traditions part on how confessing stands to forgiveness (Ps 32:5; 1 John 1:9), the page takes no side.

rows.label: The sin offering; a sacrifice for sin
rows.note: The Hebrew חַטָּאת is both “sin” and “sin offering”, and the Berean prints “sin offering” in these verses. Rom 8:3 (“as an offering for sin”) and Hebrews 5-13 (“a sacrifice for sin”) speak of an offering for sin in the same words in English. Rom 8:3 is here because the Berean prints “as an offering for sin”; the Greek there is περὶ ἁμαρτίας, “concerning sin”, the phrase the Greek Old Testament also uses for the sin offering, and translations differ on whether to render it as an offering. Where traditions part on what such a sacrifice does, and on whether the Old Testament sacrifices are fulfilled, ended or continued, the page takes no side and the Sacrifice page holds the longer account. The offering is for חַטָּאת only; עָוֺן and פֶּשַׁע are not words for an offering, and their verses stand in the other rows.
rows._why: by hand: every verse where the Berean prints 'sin offering' (114, from the Berean text of the whole Bible), plus the seven where it prints 'an offering for sin', 'a sacrifice for sin' or 'sacrifices for sins' (Rom 8:3; Heb 5:1, 5:3, 7:27, 10:12, 10:18, 13:11). A rule could not tell the offering from the sin in חַטָּאת. Ezra 6:17 is the Aramaic חַטָּאָה. The Greek of Rom 8:3 added to the note on the panel's word (review 2026-10-25); the Greek of the Hebrews verses is not stated because it was not checked. Rework 2026-10-25: the last sentence of the note, because the hub now holds the other two Hebrew words and a reader should not take the offering for them

rows.label: Iniquity, transgression and sin forgiven, atoned for, covered, wiped away, cleansed, taken away, removed, passed over, not counted against

not_verses.Hos.10.8: 'Cover us!' is the people's cry to the mountains, not sin covered
not_verses.Isa.26.21: 'cover its slain' is the earth covering the dead, not sin covered
not_verses.Lev.17.16: 'if he does not wash his clothes ... he will bear his iniquity' is a bodily washing, not sin washed away; the verse stands in the row for bearing
not_verses.Job.31.33: 'covered my transgressions like Adam by hiding my guilt' is concealing a sin, the opposite of its being covered by God
not_verses.Prov.28.13: 'conceals his sins' is concealing, not covering by God; the verse stands in the row for confessing

rows.note: Each verse holds a word of wrongdoing and one of the text's words for putting it away: forgive, make atonement, cover, wipe away, cleanse, wash, take away, remove, pass over, not count or hold against. The Hebrew nouns are three: Ps 32:1 sets “transgressions” (פֶּשַׁע) forgiven beside “sins” covered, and Ps 32:2 “the man whose iniquity (עָוֺן) the LORD does not count against him”; Ps 103:12 is “so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (פֶּשַׁע; the Hebrew verb is “make far”, רָחַק), and the forgiveness page holds it with its neighbours in the row “Sins put away”; Zech 3:4 is “I have removed your iniquity” (עָוֺן) and Zech 3:9 “I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day”; Isa 6:7 and Ps 65:3 have atonement for iniquity and transgression; Mic 7:18 “passes over the transgression” and Ezek 18:22 “None of the transgressions he has committed will be held against him” (פֶּשַׁע). Isa 1:18 and Zech 13:1 are “sins” made white and “cleansed” (חַטָּאת). Heb 10:4 and 10:11 say what the sacrifices can never do. The verbs “forgive” (Gen 50:17; Exod 34:7; Mic 7:18; Isa 33:24) and “take away” (Hos 14:2) are the Hebrew נָשָׂא, “lift, bear”; the row for that verb is below. Heb 9:15 is here for its redemption: “now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant” (the Greek is ἀπολύτρωσις, “redemption”, from παράβασις, “transgression”). A few verses in the row say the opposite or ask: Isa 22:14 (“this sin of yours will never be atoned for”), 1 Sam 3:14 (“shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering”), Matt 12:31 and Mark 3:29 (“will not be forgiven”, “will never be forgiven”) say it is not put away; Jer 18:23 (“Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin”) and Ps 109:14 (“never be blotted out”) ask that it not be; Josh 22:17 says “we have not cleansed ourselves”; Prov 20:9 asks “Who can say ... I am cleansed from my sin?”; and Prov 10:12 (“love covers all transgressions”) and Prov 17:9 (“conceals an offense”) are one person covering another's offense. Where traditions part on what an offering does for sin (covers, atones, appeases, cleanses), the page takes no side.
rows._why: נָשָׂא 'lift, bear' was in the first draft and is out of the rule: it took 'bear his sin' (Lev 24:15), 'set his heart on' (Deut 24:15; Hos 4:8) and 'bear your disgrace' (Ezek 16:52). The taken-away verses the rule cannot reach are added by hand (2 Sam 12:13 'The LORD has taken away your sin'; Ps 25:18; John 1:29; 1 John 3:5). Review 2026-10-25: half B asked to take the verses also in the sin-offering row out of this one; held for the editor. Rework 2026-10-25, by hand, each read in the Berean: Ps 103:12 ('removed our transgressions', רָחַק hiphil: no rule reaches it, since 'remove' is not among the rule's words and רָחַק alone would take every 'far from'); Mic 7:19 ('cast all our sins into the depths of the sea') and Isa 38:17 ('cast all my sins behind Your back') for the same picture, as the forgiveness hub's row does; Zech 3:4 ('I have removed your iniquity'); Job 7:21 ('pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity'); the נָשָׂא verses where the Berean itself prints forgive, pardon or take away: Gen 50:17, Exod 34:7, Num 14:18, Mic 7:18, Isa 33:24, Hos 14:2, Isa 40:2 ('her iniquity has been pardoned'), 2 Sam 24:10 ('take away the iniquity of Your servant'). The rule alone brings in Ps 32:1, 32:5, 51:1-2, 65:3, Isa 6:7, 27:9, 43:25 and Jer 31:34, 33:8, 50:20. Four verses the rule took on the new words are taken out by hand (Isa 26:21, Lev 17:16, Job 31:33, Prov 28:13; reasons in not_verses), and several verses in the row say 'not' (Isa 22:14 'will not be atoned for', 1 Sam 3:14, Jer 18:23, Ps 109:14, Josh 24:19): hard verses stay, and the panel should read them there. Second pass the same day, after the first build left 199 noun verses under More: read in the Berean and added where the verse puts the wrongdoing away or declines to count it: 1 Chr 21:8 ('take away the iniquity of Your servant'), Ps 32:2 ('does not count against him', the verse Rom 4:8 quotes), Ezek 18:22 and 33:16 ('held against him'), Num 12:11 ('do not hold against us this sin'), Isa 1:18, Zech 13:1 and Zech 3:9; Acts 7:60, Isa 64:9, Rom 11:27, 1 Pet 4:8, 1 Sam 25:28 and Rom 3:25 are the same kind (the label gained 'passed over, not counted against' for Mic 7:18, Rom 3:25 and these).

rows.label: The sins of the kings: “the sin Jeroboam caused Israel to commit”, “caused Judah to sin”; Baasha, Manasseh
rows.note: The same phrase, “the sins of Jeroboam” or “the sin he caused Israel to commit”, closes the verdict on a king of Israel again and again in Kings, in the noun (“his sin”) and in the verb (“caused Israel to sin”); 1 Kgs 12:30 says where it began, and 1 Kgs 16:13 and 2 Kgs 21:16 are the sins of Baasha and Manasseh, who “caused Judah to sin” (2 Kgs 21:11). Jer 32:35 says the same of Judah. The word is חַטָּאת, “sin”, throughout; the verses are listed as written.
rows._why: review 2026-10-25: the noun row (rule: a sin word and Jeroboam in one verse, 21 verses, nine added by hand) and the verb row 'He caused Israel to sin' (15 verses) shared nine verses and were one phrase split by part of speech; they are one row now. A pick, because a rule row takes only noun-form verses and five of the verb row's verses are verb-only: 1 Kgs 21:22 (Ahab), 22:52 (Ahaziah), 2 Kgs 21:11 (Manasseh), 23:15 (Josiah breaks down the altar Jeroboam 'had caused Israel to sin' by), Jer 32:35. The 30 noun verses are the first build's, unchanged. Rework 2026-10-25: unchanged but for the last sentence of the note; the kings' phrase is the sin word alone

rows.label: The calf at Sinai: “a great sin”, “their sin”, “that sinful thing”
rows.note: The verses that name the sin of the golden calf. Moses asks Aaron “that you have led them into so great a sin?” (Exod 32:21), tells the people “You have committed a great sin” (32:30) and says to the LORD “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed!” (32:31); 32:32 is “if You would only forgive their sin”, and 32:34 “I will punish them for their sin”. Retelling it, Moses speaks of “all the sin you had committed” (Deut 9:18) and of “that sinful thing, the calf you had made” (Deut 9:21). Exod 32:30 and 32:32 are also in the row for sin forgiven and atoned for, and Exod 32:34 in the row for sin and its consequence.
rows._why: ruled 2026-10-25 (rulings sheet, as recommended): one scene was scattered, with Exod 32:30 and 32:32 in the forgiven row and the other five only under More. A pick of seven verses, each read in the Berean. The row is not called 'Sin first named' and there is no Day of Atonement row, as ruled. The 25th row became the 26th with the rows added since

rows.label: Sin and its consequence: “die in your sin”, “the wages of sin is death”, “sevenfold for your sins”, “bear the consequences of his sin”

not_verses.Jer.18.23: 'plots to kill me' is the prophet's enemies' plot, not sin and death
not_verses.Rev.1.5: 'the firstborn from the dead' is Christ's resurrection, a different clause from 'freed us from our sins'
not_verses.Heb.9.15: the death in the verse redeems from transgressions ('He has died to redeem them from the transgressions'); it is not a consequence of sin, and the verse stands in the row for sin forgiven (panel-2)

rows.note: The text puts sin and what comes of it in one verse in several ways: death (“die in your sin”, “the wages of sin is death”, “died to sin”, “they will incur guilt and die”) and punishment (“sevenfold for your sins”, plunder, being swept away, bearing it). The Hebrew verses now include iniquity and transgression: “will waste away in their iniquity” (Lev 26:39), “I will attend to their transgression with the rod, and to their iniquity with stripes” (Ps 89:32), “you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away” (Isa 50:1), “through their iniquities, suffered affliction” (Ps 107:17), “so that your iniquity will not become your downfall” (Ezek 18:30). Amos 1:3-2:6 has the formula “For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment” (פֶּשַׁע, “transgression”, seven times), and Amos 3:2 and 3:14 “I will punish you for all your iniquities”, “the day I punish Israel for their transgressions”. Lam 1:5 (“grief because of her many transgressions”), Isa 64:7 (“delivered us into the hand of our iniquity”), Ezek 39:23-24, Ezra 9:7 and 9:13 (“punished us less than our iniquities deserve”), Hos 9:7 and Josh 22:20 (“it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin”) say the same of a people or a man. The page lists them and does not say how they relate. In Num 18:22 the Berean prints “incur guilt”; the Hebrew words there are “bear”, “sin” and “die”. Rom 8:10 (“your body is dead because of sin”) is here too. Isa 53:8 (“stricken for the transgression of My people”) and Isa 53:12 (“He bore the sin of many”) are here, and Isa 53:12 is also in the row for sin carried or lifted; they name no one, and where traditions part on whom they speak of, the page takes no side. The sin that is forgiven is in the row for forgiveness.
rows._why: review 2026-10-25: 'Sin and death' (a rule on death words, 41 verses) and 'Sin and what follows' (17 verses by hand) both name a consequence in the verse with the sin; merged, with the first row's rule and the second's verses added. The examples are Ezek 18:24 and 2 Sam 12:13 first so that the Hebrew Scriptures are heard first. Rev 18:5 (her sins 'piled up to heaven') is no longer an example because it does not show 'bear the consequences'. Rework 2026-10-25: the death rule now takes the iniquity and transgression verses that name death (Ezek 18:17 'will not die for his father's iniquity', Num 27:3, Jer 31:30 and the like); five verses read in the Berean are added by hand where the consequence is named without a death word (Lev 26:39; Ps 89:32; Ps 107:17; Isa 50:1; Ezek 18:30). Where עָוֺן means the punishment itself (Gen 4:13) the verse is not counted. Second pass the same day, after the first build left 199 noun verses under More: thirty-two more verses where the consequence is named in the verse with the wrongdoing (the Amos formula, Lam 1:5, 1:22, Isa 13:11, 53:8, 64:6-7, Josh 22:20, Num 32:23, Ezek 4:17, 24:23, 33:6, 39:23-24, Ezra 9:7, 9:13, Hos 5:5, 9:7, 14:1, Exod 32:34, Jer 13:22, 25:12, Heb 2:2, Neh 9:37), all read in the Berean except Amos 1:6, 1:9, 1:11, 1:13 and 2:1, which repeat Amos 1:3's formula in the Hebrew. Isa 53:8 ('stricken for the transgression of My people') names no one, and the page takes no side on whom it speaks of

rows.label: Sin and the law, the commandment

not_verses.Acts.13.38: the Greek's 13:38 carries 'the law of Moses' that the Berean prints in 13:39; 13:38 as shown has no 'law'
not_verses.Lev.6.25: 'the law of the sin offering' is a ritual rule, shown in the row for the sin offering
not_verses.Lev.7.7: 'the same law applies to both' is a ritual rule, shown in the row for the sin offering
not_verses.Lev.7.37: 'the law of the burnt offering ... the sin offering' is a ritual rule, shown in the row for the sin offering

rows.note: Rom 7:7 asks “Is the law sin?” and answers in the verse; Rom 3:20 and 1 Cor 15:56 say the law brings awareness of sin and gives sin its power; 1 John 3:4 says “sin is lawlessness”. The Greek words for “transgression” (παράβασις, Rom 2:23; 4:15; Gal 3:19) and “transgressor” (παραβάτης, Rom 2:25, 27; Jas 2:9, 11) are here where the verse names the law; the Berean prints some of them “breaking the law” and “lawbreaker”, and the example is marked with the Greek word it stands on. The verses are set out as written. The Hebrew verses here say what the law forbids and what breaking it is: breaking the commandment (Num 15:31, “he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment”), rejecting the Law of the LORD (Amos 2:4), and not turning from iniquities, though “it is written in the Law of Moses” (Dan 9:13); in Mal 2:6 the Berean's “true instruction” (תּוֹרָה) turned many from iniquity. Two of the examples are Hebrew (Num 15:31; Dan 9:13) and two Greek.

rows.label: Sin through one man; sinful from conception
rows.note: One of three rows set side by side with the two after it. Where Christian traditions part on original sin and inherited guilt, the page takes no side and ranks none of the three above another. Adam is named in Rom 5:14, where the word is παράβασις, “transgression”, the Berean's “the likeness of the transgression of Adam”; Ps 51:5 is David's own confession, and the Hebrew there is עָוֺן, “iniquity” (“I was brought forth in iniquity”), beside חֵטְא, “sinful”. The two rows after this one hold Old Testament verses on who bears a person's sin, and the disciples' question about the man born blind with the Pharisees' answer to him (John 9:2-3, 9:34); they are set beside this row because readers bring them to it, not because they ask the question of original sin themselves. Gen 8:21, Job 14:4, Ps 58:3 and Eph 2:3 are often read with these and hold none of this hub's words, so they are not shown.
rows._why: by hand: each verse says the thing in its label in the Berean's words. Rom 5:13 ('sin was in the world before the law') and Rom 5:20-21 ('where sin increased', 'sin reigned in death') are not about one man and stay in their own rows. Rom 5:14 names Adam; 5:16 'one man's sin'; 5:19 'the many were made sinners' (the adjective). Review 2026-10-25: John 9:34 moved to the next row to stand with John 9:2-3, and 'born in utter sin' left the label because the Pharisees' retort is not a claim the text makes. Rework 2026-10-25: Ps 51:5's Hebrew words named (iniquity and sin) and Rom 5:14's παράβασις named in the note; no verse added

rows.label: “Each is to die for his own sin”; the son does not bear the father's; “who sinned, this man or his parents?”
rows.note: The second of three rows set side by side; the page takes no side. The text asks who bears a person's sin: the one who sinned, or his father or his children (Deut 24:16; 2 Kgs 14:6; Ezek 18:4, 18:20). Num 27:3 is a man who “died because of his own sin”. Jer 31:30 (“each will die for his own iniquity”) and Ezek 18:17-20 (“will not die for his father's iniquity”; “Why shouldn't the son bear the iniquity of his father?”) say it in the Hebrew עָוֺן, “iniquity”, which the Berean prints “iniquity” and, in Ezek 18:19, as the people's question. John 9:2-3 is the disciples' question and Jesus' answer about a man born blind, and John 9:34 is the Pharisees' retort to the man, which follows Jesus' answer. Ezek 18:14, a son who does not do as his father did, is in the next row.
rows._why: by hand: Ezek 18:4 and 18:20 have the verb ('the soul who sins') and 18:20 also 'the iniquity of his father'; John 9:2-3 have the verb. John 9:34 added in the review of 2026-10-25 so that the scene stands whole (the Berean: 'You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?'); it is not among the examples, as it does not show this label. Ezek 18:14 stays in the next row. Rework 2026-10-25: Jer 31:30, Ezek 18:17 and Ezek 18:19 added (read in the Berean) now that עָוֺן is a word of the hub; the note had said Jer 31:30 'is not counted here'

rows.label: The fathers' sins, and the children
rows.note: The third of three rows set side by side; the page takes no side. Exod 34:7, Exod 20:5, Deut 5:9, Num 14:18 and Jer 32:18 say the LORD visits (“punishes”, “repays”) the iniquity of the fathers on their children, the Hebrew עָוֺן, “iniquity”, which the Berean prints “iniquity” and in Jer 32:18 “iniquity” too. The generations confess their fathers' sins with their own (Lev 26:40; Jer 14:20; Neh 9:2; Dan 9:16; Ps 106:6) and ask that they not be remembered (Ps 79:8; Ps 109:14 asks the opposite of an enemy); Jer 11:10 and Isa 65:7 name the fathers' iniquities beside the people's own; in Lam 5:7 they say “we bear their punishment”; Ezek 18:14 is a son who sees his father's sins and does not do likewise, and Ezek 18:19 is the people's question about it.
rows._why: by hand. The label says only what the verses say; none says that guilt passes down and none says it does not. Jer 14:20 'the guilt of our fathers; indeed, we have sinned against You'; Lam 5:7 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment' (a complaint, not a confession, review 2026-10-25). Rework 2026-10-25: Exod 20:5, Deut 5:9, Num 14:18, Lev 26:39-40, Ps 79:8, Ps 109:14, Isa 65:7, Jer 11:10, Jer 32:18 and Ezek 18:19 added, each read in the Berean, now that עָוֺן is a word of the hub; the first round's note had said Exod 20:5 and Num 14:18 'are not counted here'

rows.label: “All under sin”, “slaves to sin”, “dead in your trespasses and sins”
rows.note: The first of three rows on how sin holds a person and how the text speaks of resisting it, set side by side with the next two; readers sometimes call this question total depravity, and the page takes no side on it. Rom 7:14 is also in the Romans 7 row, where readers part on who the “I” is. Rom 8:10 (“your body is dead because of sin”) is in the row on sin and its consequence.
rows._why: by hand: each verse says it in the Berean's words. Rom 8:10 was in this row and left it in the review of 2026-10-25, being the body's death in a believer and not slavery; it stays in the consequence row. Rom 7:14 'sold as a slave to sin' stays: it fits the label and is the contested verse

rows.label: Sin to be mastered, resisted, thrown off: “you must master it”, “sin shall not be your master”, “set free from sin”, “dead to sin”
rows.note: The second of three rows on how sin holds a person and how the text speaks of resisting it. The row before has the verses of sin as a master; this row has the verses that speak of mastering it (Gen 4:7: “sin is crouching at your door ... you must master it”), of not letting it reign, of being set free from it, and of resisting it and throwing it off (Heb 12:1, 12:4). Gen 4:7 is the LORD's word to Cain, and Rom 6 and Heb 12 are written to the readers of those letters; the verbs are of the same kind (master, reign, free), and the text does not say that they are one act. The page takes no side on how the two fit together.
rows._why: by hand: Gen 4:7 is the Old Testament's own word to Cain; Rom 6 is Paul's. Rom 6:10 ('He died to sin once for all') is of Christ and stays in the Christ row. The 16-verse check found Heb 12:4 ('In your struggle against sin') under a label that named only mastering and being set free; the label now says 'resisted, thrown off', which Heb 12:1 and 12:4 say. Review 2026-10-25 asked that Gen 4:7 be the stated lead (it is the first example) and that the note say to whom each is said

rows.label: “Sin living in me”: Romans 7
rows.note: The third of three rows on how sin holds a person and how the text speaks of resisting it. Readers part on who the “I” of Rom 7:14-25 is: Paul before he knew Christ, Paul as a believer, or a person under the law whom the passage does not name; the page takes no side. Rom 8:2 (“set you free from the law of sin and death”) is in the row before.
rows._why: by hand, so that the passage stands as one: the verses of Rom 7 where 'sin' is the subject or the master.

rows.label: A sin that leads to death; a sin that is not forgiven
rows.note: 1 John 5:16-17 speaks of “a sin that leads to death” and “sin that does not lead to death”; Mark 3:28-29 and Matt 12:31 set all sins and blasphemies forgiven beside blasphemy against the Spirit, which “will not be forgiven”. What the sin to death is, whether the death is bodily or of the soul, and what the blasphemy is, readers take differently, and the page takes no side. Heb 10:26 (sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth) is in the verb form.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that say it. Luke 12:10 and Heb 6:4-6, often read with these, hold none of this hub's words and are not shown; the forgiveness hub has the blasphemy verses with their own row. Review 2026-10-25: half B asked that Heb 10:26 move here; held for the editor

rows.label: Christ and our sins: “save His people from their sins”, “died for”, “bore”, “takes away”, “knew no sin”
rows.note: Each verse speaks of Jesus and sin, and the text names him in it or in the sentence it belongs to: Matt 1:21 and John 1:29 by name, Heb 1:3 as “the Son”, John 8:46 and Matt 26:28 in his own words (“Me”, “My blood”), and the rest by “Christ” or “He” (1 Pet 2:24; Gal 1:4). The verses say he “died for”, “bore”, “takes away”, “was made” sin, “knew no sin”, “was without sin”. Where traditions part on what his death does about sin, the page takes no side. 1 Pet 2:24 says He “bore our sins”; Isa 53:12 says “He bore the sin of many” and Lev 16:21 puts the sins “on the goat's head”; Isa 53:12 and Lev 16:22 are in the row “Sin carried or lifted”, Isa 53:12 also in “Sin and its consequence”, and Lev 16:21 in the rows “Confessing sin, iniquity, transgression” and “Iniquity, transgression and sin side by side”; 1 Pet 2:24, John 1:29, Heb 9:28 and 1 John 3:5 stand in both this row and “Sin carried or lifted”, this row for the person they speak of and that row for the verb. The page does not say how the three relate.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: a rule on 'Christ' would take every verse near the name. The sinless verses (John 8:46; 2 Cor 5:21; Heb 4:15; 1 Pet 2:22; 1 John 3:5) stand here with the died-for verses because the text sets them together (1 John 3:5 'appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin'; 2 Cor 5:21). Isa 53:12 ('bore the sin of many') names no one and is in the consequence row by the rule. Review 2026-10-25: the label opens with Matt 1:21's words ('save His people from their sins') so that its first example shows it; nothing else in the row was changed. Rework 2026-10-25: unchanged; Isa 53:5, 53:11-12 (the Hebrew words are פֶּשַׁע, עָוֺן and חֵטְא) now stand in the rows by rule and in the next row, and name no one; the held request to point to Isaiah 53 from this row is still the editor's

rows.label: Sin carried or lifted: “bear his iniquity”, “forgiving iniquity”, “the goat will carry on itself all their iniquities”, “bore the sin of many”, “takes away the sin of the world”
rows.note: The Hebrew נָשָׂא is “lift, carry, bear”, and the text uses it of sin in two ways the English has to choose between: to bear it (Lev 5:1, “he shall bear the iniquity”; Lev 16:22, “The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities”; Num 14:34; Ezek 4:4-6; Isa 53:12, “He bore the sin of many”) and to lift it from someone, which the Berean prints “forgive” or “pardon” (Exod 34:7, “forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin”; Mic 7:18; Ps 32:5, “You forgave the guilt of my sin”; Isa 33:24; 1 Sam 25:28, “Please forgive your servant's offense”; Exod 23:21, “he will not forgive rebellion”). In the Law the priests bear iniquity as part of their service: the plate on Aaron's forehead, “so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things” (Exod 28:38); Aaron, his sons and his father's house “must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary”, and Aaron and his sons “the iniquity involving your priesthood” (Num 18:1); the Levites “must bear their iniquity” (Num 18:23). The page does not say what the text means by it. Five verses use other words for bearing: Isa 53:11 (“He will bear their iniquities”) and Lam 5:7 (“we bear their punishment”) have the Hebrew סָבַל, “bear”; Isa 53:6 (“the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all”) has הִפְגִּיעַ, “laid”, and is here with the verses that speak of sin as carried by another; Heb 9:28 (“to bear the sins of many”) and 1 Pet 2:24 (“bore our sins”) have the Greek ἀναφέρω, “bear”. They are here because the verse says sin is borne or laid, and the page does not say these words are the one verb. The Greek αἴρω, “lift, take away”, is John 1:29 and 1 John 3:5. John 1:29, 1 John 3:5, Heb 9:28 and 1 Pet 2:24 are also in the row “Christ and our sins”: there for the person they speak of, here for the verb. The page sets the verses together under the verb and does not decide, in any verse, which of the two the Hebrew means; where the Berean decides, the verse is also in the row for forgiveness. Isa 53:11-12 name no one, and where traditions part on whom they speak of, the page takes no side.
rows._why: rework 2026-10-25: a rule on the verb whose object is a word of the hub (the frames' patient), so only 'bear/lift/take away + sin, iniquity, transgression'. נָשָׂא is not in the forgiven row's rule because it also means 'bear' and 'set the heart on' (see that row); here it is the row's whole point, with the Hebrew two meanings side by side as the Hebrew has them. Added as the 25th row because the נָשָׂא verses are a large and distinct group (the text's own idiom 'bear his iniquity') that fit no existing row: the consequence row is about what follows sin, not the verb. Three verses added by hand in the second pass because the frames record no object for them: 1 Sam 25:28 and Exod 23:21 (the Hebrew object is led by לְ, 'forgive the transgression'), and Isa 53:6 (another verb)

rows.label: “There is no one who does not sin”; “all have sinned”; “if we say we have not sinned”
rows.note: The first of three rows on whether a believer sins, set beside the two after it. In the Hebrew Scriptures “no one without sin” is said of every human being (1 Kgs 8:46; Eccl 7:20; Prov 20:9). 1 John 1:8-10 speak to believers (“we”); Jer 2:35 is a people who say “I have not sinned”. Where Christian traditions part on whether a believer sins, and how 1 John 1:8 and 3:9 fit together, the page takes no side. 1 John 2:1 is in the commands row.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that say no one is without sin, or that deny having sinned. Prov 20:9 and 1 John 1:8 have the noun ('pure from my sin', 'we have no sin'), the others the verb; the text sets them with the same thought. 1 John 2:1 left this row in the review of 2026-10-25: it says 'so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate' and names no universal sinning

rows.label: “Anyone born of God ... cannot go on sinning”
rows.note: The second of three rows on whether a believer sins. The Berean reads 1 John 3:6 “keeps on sinning”, 3:9 “cannot go on sinning” and 5:18 “does not keep on sinning”; the Greek verb is in the present tense, and readers part on whether this means a continuing practice or no sin at all, and on whether it describes every believer. The page takes no side and sets it beside 1 John 1:8-10 in the row before and the commands in the row after.
rows._why: by hand: only the three verses that say it. 1 John 3:8 (the devil has been sinning) is not of a believer and stays in More

rows.label: “Do not sin”, “sin no more”, “stop sinning”
rows.note: The third of three rows on whether a believer sins: the commands. In the Hebrew Scriptures they are said to the people (Exod 20:20) and in the Psalms (Ps 4:4; 119:11); in the Gospels and letters to those addressed (John 5:14; 8:11; Eph 4:26; 1 John 2:1). Ps 4:4 and Eph 4:26 are the same words (“be angry, yet do not sin”); John 8:11 is said to the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53-8:11 is a passage the earliest manuscripts lack, and the site marks it wherever it is shown). The page takes no side on how the commands and the two rows before them stand to each other.
rows._why: by hand: the commands and warnings in the verb's own words. Rom 6:15 'Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!' is a question and is here because its answer is 'Certainly not'

rows.label: Sinned, transgressed, rebelled against the LORD, against God
rows.note: The verses where the text itself names the LORD, God or the Most High as the one sinned against: “I have sinned against the LORD”, “sin against God”, “the LORD, against whom we have sinned”. Isa 1:2 (“the LORD has spoken: ... they have rebelled against Me”), Jer 2:29 (“You have all rebelled against Me,” declares the LORD) and Jer 3:13 (“you have rebelled against the LORD your God”) are the Hebrew פָּשַׁע, “rebel, transgress”, a word beside חָטָא, “sin”; Isa 59:13 has “rebelling and denying the LORD”. Three verses say only “against You” and have the name close by: Ps 51:4 (“Against You, You only, have I sinned”) in the same prayer as “O God” (Ps 51:1, “Have mercy on me, O God”), Ps 119:11 (“that I might not sin against You”) beside “Blessed are You, O LORD” (Ps 119:12), and 1 Kgs 8:46 (“When they sin against You”) two verses after “they pray to the LORD” (1 Kgs 8:44); each is here beside the verse that names him and also stays in its other row. Verses that say only “against You” where the name is further off (1 Kgs 8:33; 2 Chr 6:24, with “O LORD my God” in 1 Kgs 8:28 and 2 Chr 6:19) or “against Me” (Exod 23:33; Hos 4:7; Ezek 14:13) are in the other rows or under More: the page names no one where the verse does not.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: a rule on 'the LORD' as the one sinned against would take every verse near a name. Each verse names him: Gen 20:6 'Then God said', Gen 39:9 'against God', Exod 32:33 'The LORD replied', Judg 10:10 'cried out to the LORD', Ps 41:4 'O LORD', Jer 14:20 'O LORD', Dan 9:8 'O LORD', Mic 7:9 'the rage of the LORD', Ps 78:17 'the Most High'. 1 Sam 2:25 stands also in the row for another person. The row for the pronoun verses was dropped (the first build had it, 16 verses) to keep the hub near 25 rows; they are under More and in 'I have sinned' (Ps 51:4). Review 2026-10-25: half B asked that Ps 51:4, 1 Kgs 8:33, 8:46 and 2 Chr 6:24 be added by hand; held for the editor, as a change to a row about God. Rework 2026-10-25: the פָּשַׁע verses where the verse itself names the LORD (Isa 1:2 'the LORD has spoken', Jer 2:29 'declares the LORD', Jer 3:13 'the LORD your God', Isa 59:13 'denying the LORD'), each read in the Berean; the label gained 'transgressed, rebelled'. The other פָּשַׁע verses say only 'Me' or 'You' or name no one and are under More

rows.label: Sinned against another: a neighbor, a brother, one's own body
rows.note: People sinning against people, in the Law and Prophets, the Gospels and the letters. In Luke 15:18 and 15:21 the son says “against heaven and against you”, and the page lets the words stand. 1 Cor 8:12 adds “you sin against Christ”, and 1 Cor 6:18 sins “against his own body”.
rows._why: by hand: each verse names the one wronged, a person or the speaker's own body. Matt 18:15 and 18:21 'sins against you', 'sins against me' are the brother; Luke 11:4 'everyone who sins against us'. Review 2026-10-25: half B asked that 1 Cor 8:12 and the 'against heaven' halves of Luke 15:18, 21 move out; held for the editor

rows.label: “I have sinned”, “we have sinned”, “we have sinned and rebelled”
rows.note: The words a person or a people say of themselves. They are said by Pharaoh (Exod 9:27), Balaam (Num 22:34), Saul (1 Sam 15:24), David (2 Sam 12:13; 24:10), Judas (Matt 27:4) and the prodigal son (Luke 15:21), and by the people together; the page lists them and does not say which of them were heard. Lam 3:42, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven”, is the people's word; the Berean's “sinned” there is the Hebrew פָּשַׁע, “transgressed”.
rows._why: by hand: the first-person verses of the verb in the Berean's words ('I have sinned', 'we have sinned'). Rework 2026-10-25: Lam 3:42 added now that פָּשַׁע is a word of the hub (the Berean 'We have sinned and rebelled', read) and the label gained 'we have transgressed'. Review panel-2 (2026-10-25): no verse's English prints 'we have transgressed' (Lam 3:42 prints 'sinned and rebelled'), so the label is now 'we have sinned and rebelled', Lam 3:42 is an example, and the note says the Hebrew word

rows.label: “If someone sins”: the Law's cases, sinning unintentionally; sinning defiantly (Num 15:30); sinning deliberately (Heb 10:26)
rows.note: The Law's cases begin “If someone sins”: Lev 4:2, 4:22, 4:27 and 5:15 “sins unintentionally”, Lev 5:1 by failing to testify, 5:17 “even though he was unaware”, 6:2-4 by deceiving his neighbor, Lev 4:3 the anointed priest. Num 15:30 speaks of the person who “sins defiantly”, the Hebrew “does with a high hand”, and is shown here although the Hebrew verb there is not חָטָא. Heb 10:26 speaks of those who “deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth”; it is a verse of Hebrews and not one of the Law's cases, and the page does not say that Hebrews applies Num 15:30. Readers part on whether Heb 10:26-27 describes a believer who falls away or one who never believed, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the Law's verses that begin with the verb in the Berean's words ('If someone sins ...', 'sins unintentionally', 'once he has sinned'), and the two that say 'defiantly' and 'deliberately'. Num 15:30 is added from the Berean's English, and its note says so. Review 2026-10-25: both halves found the old label ('the Law's cases ... sinning deliberately') made Heb 10:26 a Law case; the label now names the three kinds and the verses that carry them. Half B's move of Heb 10:26 to the row on the sin not forgiven is held for the editor

rows.label: Sinners, often set beside the righteous or the wicked
rows.note: The text sets sinners beside the righteous: “sinners will not stand in the assembly of the righteous”, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners”, “the many were made sinners ... the many will be made righteous” (Rom 5:19, which is also in the row on sin through one man, where the page takes no side). In the Law and the Psalms the sinners are also named beside the wicked: the men of Sodom “wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD” (Gen 13:13), “May sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more” (Ps 104:35).
rows._why: review 2026-10-25: the first build dropped an Old Testament 'sinners' row to stay near 25; half B asked for its verses to be folded in here so the Gospels' 'tax collectors and sinners' is not met without the category it contrasts with. Matt 9:13 stays in the row by the rule and in the Christ row, and is no longer an example here

rows.label: Christ Jesus and sinners: tax collectors and sinners, “came into the world to save sinners”
rows.note: By hand, the verses where a sinner or the sinners are named beside Jesus or Christ in the verse or the scene: he eats with them and is called their friend, he comes to call them, he is delivered into their hands, he died for them, he is set apart from them. Where the verse says “the Son of Man” or “Me” the scene names Jesus (Matt 9:10; Mark 14:41).
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are. The tax collectors and sinners rule (τελώνης) gave 9 verses, all of them in this list
